items.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: So I went to New York and I learned from other musicians I was working with, Duke Ellington, working with Count Basie, and big bands. Ray Charles.

ctx.x: Still the 12-bar blues. And sometimes, like Ray Charles, sometimes the 12-bar blues would be extended to 16 bars you know, and then you would hear, if you played for church you would hear the same format in churches playing the same formal changes. In fact the church, in the Baptist church, they usually adapt to the music or sound that’s popular and then put spiritual words on top of that. You know if you have a big popular tune that’s in the psyche of everybody they would actually put, somebody would construct a…

the same music, you know it’s the same format. So the original R & B, rhythm & blues, was like popular music, 40s and 50s, and I mean the popular music not only blues stuff like Little Richard, but I’m talking about Cole Porter, Rogers & Hart, Gershwin. Those were the major composers at that particular time. And we took those tunes and dressed them up, instead of doing swing we’d play bossa nova, we’d play Latin, we’d play shuffle and change the beat.
